---
title: "Integrated chemistry workshop"
---

Allow 90–120 minutes. Work independently, compare explanations in pairs and
then inspect the checks. Use drawings, words and quantitative evidence together.

## Case 1. One molecule, several transformations

Lactic acid is CH₃CH(OH)COOH. It is encountered in biological contexts, but this
case requires only its drawn functional groups.

1. Identify its alcohol type, acid group and stereocentre.
2. Draw hydroxide deprotonation of its carboxyl group with two arrows.
3. Draw the product of oxidising the secondary alcohol to a ketone.
4. Draw the target ester made from its acid group and ethanol.
5. For each change, state whether it changes bonding at the original
   stereocentre and whether that centre still qualifies for R/S assignment.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Draw every relevant oxygen and hydrogen. Ask whether the central carbon has
four different substituents and remains tetrahedral after the transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked comparison"}
The alcohol is secondary and the CH(OH) carbon is the stereocentre. Hydroxide
gives CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻ and water without changing the centre's bonds. Oxidation
gives CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid; the former centre is now planar and is not
R/S. Esterification at the acid gives CH₃CH(OH)COOCH₂CH₃ plus water as a net
equilibrium transformation; the alcohol-bearing centre remains tetrahedral.
These drawings specify target changes, not a promise of perfect selectivity
under all conditions. Ordinary proton transfer at the carboxyl OH alone does
not invert the stereocentre.
:::

## Case 2. Configuration is not a drawing direction

Draw both configurations of lactic acid with one wedged and one dashed bond.
Assign priorities OH > COOH > CH₃ > H, explain the COOH/CH₃ tie-break and
assign R or S for your own drawings. Redraw one molecule after rotating the
whole drawing; verify that the configuration stays the same. Can you infer
the sign of optical rotation from that R/S label?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked reasoning"}
O outranks C, and H is lowest. For the two carbon substituents compare their
next attached atoms: the acid carbon is treated as attached to O,O,O in CIP
multiple-bond bookkeeping, while methyl carbon is attached to H,H,H. Orient
the lowest-priority group away; 1→2→3 clockwise is R and anticlockwise is S.
If the lowest-priority group points toward you, reverse the apparent result.
Rigid rotation preserves configuration. R/S does not determine the sign or
size of measured optical rotation.
:::

## Case 3. Resolve an unknown with several observations

An unknown has C₄H₈O₂; its complete simulated IR has C=O but no broad O–H.
Its simulated proton NMR has 1.25 ppm triplet (3H), 2.05 ppm singlet (3H)
and 4.12 ppm quartet (2H). Compare ethyl ethanoate, butanoic acid and a
hydroxyketone. For each candidate make at least one testable prediction;
then explain which candidate best fits the supplied set.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked interpretation"}
Ethyl ethanoate fits an ester carbonyl, O–CH₂ quartet/CH₃ triplet and acetyl
CH₃ singlet. Butanoic acid predicts a broad acid O–H feature and lacks O–CH₂;
a hydroxyketone predicts OH and needs a different proton arrangement. These
comparisons support the ester candidate among this set. Explicit assignments
are stronger than stating that the spectrum “looks like an ester”.
:::

## Case 4. Critique a tempting success claim

For the aspirin teaching reaction, theoretical mass is 1.8016 g. A student
reports 1.70 g isolate, a single TLC spot and concludes “pure product, 94%
yield”. Their IR has an unexpected feature and NMR has an extra major set of
signals. Which numerical statement follows from the mass? Which chemical
claim is unsupported? Suggest two possible explanations and a useful next
check. Do not diagnose a unique impurity from these limited facts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked critique"}
The apparent mass-based isolated yield is 100 × 1.70/1.8016 ≈ 94.4%, assuming
the isolated mass is product. Purity is unsupported. Residual solvent or a
co-migrating organic impurity are possible explanations; incomplete reaction
or mistaken assignment is also possible. Compare the full NMR integration
and signals against the expected product and appropriate references, or
repeat TLC under a suitable different separation condition. The best next
check depends on which contradictory feature can be tested most directly.
:::

## Case 5. A report someone else can inspect

Use your own Rmd project to write a short conclusion for a teaching dataset.
Include the chemical claim, two observations, the reasoning linking them,
one limitation and a proposed next observation. Reopen the project in a fresh
R session and Knit from the saved inputs. Ask a partner to find the raw values,
the calculation and the evidence supporting each sentence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Review checklist"}
The report should reconstruct its own objects, use relative paths and identify
the data as simulated when appropriate. The conclusion must distinguish
isolated yield, identity and purity and avoid treating a candidate's filename
as evidence. Reproducibility and chemical validity are separate requirements:
both must be checked. See [practical reporting](../reference/practical.qmd).
:::

Optional further reading is selected biological examples from Solomons
chapters 22–24, through the [reading guide](../reference/reading.qmd). Detailed
metabolic pathways and advanced synthesis are outside this workshop.
